questions.stem: A 17-year-old man is admitted to hospital following a road accident. His spleen is removed because it is ruptured. Which role of the spleen will be lost with its removal that may affect the patient's future health?
options: Deletion of immature autoreactive T cells
Major site of insulin producing cells
Primary lymphoid organ where immature lymphocytes arise
Removal of encapsulated bacteria by phagocytic mechanisms
Responds to the pituitary gland to produce thyroxine
questions.explanation: The spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ composed of red pulp and white pulp and a marginal zone. It has a unique role in the phagocytic removal of encapsulated bacteria.
questions.source_label: MRCS Part A: 550 SBAs and EMQs || 2nd Edition

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man scheduled for surgery was found to be HIV positive at pre-assessment. What is the most likely effect of this infection on his immune response to infection?
options: His ability to phagocytose and kill bacteria will be lost
Activation of an effective adaptive immune response will be impaired
Activation of the alternative complement pathway will be prevented
None; HIV infection does not affect the immune response
Innate immune defences will be impaired
questions.explanation: Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) selectively targets and kills CD4+ T lymphocytes. Activated CD4+ T cells provide help to CD8+ cytotoxic T-cells and B-cells in activating an adaptive immune response.
questions.source_label: MRCS Part A: 550 SBAs and EMQs || 2nd Edition

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with septicaemia due to an antibiotic resistant infection was admitted to hospital. In septicaemia, uncontrolled activation of inflammatory cytokines can lead to acute respiratory distress syndrome and multiorgan failure. What are cytokines?
options: Antigen-specific molecules produced by B lymphocytes
Part of an enzyme cascade activated by immune complexes
Small signalling proteins that regulate immune activation
Subtype of cytotoxic T cells
Ultracellular enzymes which kill bacteria within phagocytic cells
questions.explanation: Cytokines are small soluble signalling molecules that enable all immune cells to regulate themselves, each other and any cell that expresses the requisite cytokine receptor.
questions.source_label: MRCS Part A: 550 SBAs and EMQs || 2nd Edition

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman is admitted for hip replacement. She had suffered for many years from chronic rheumatoid arthritis, an autoimmune disease with progressive joint destruction. What is the most likely mechanism causing autoimmune disease?
options: The body mounts an immune response against itself
Chronic activation of allergen specific IgE sensitised mast cells initiates the disease
A deficient immune response due to the actions of an external agent
A genetic defect causing a deranged immune response
T cell activation is inhibited
questions.explanation: Autoimmune disease occurs when a genetically susceptible individual comes in contact with an environmental trigger. Immune tolerance mechanisms, which prevent recognition of self proteins by the immune system, are bypassed by a number of mechanisms and an autoimmune response occurs.
questions.source_label: MRCS Part A: 550 SBAs and EMQs || 2nd Edition

questions.stem: A 21-year-old woman is admitted to hospital for the removal of her wisdom teeth. Investigations reveal that she has high levels of circulating IgM antibody. What statement below best describes IgM antibodies?
options: Antibodies that can survive on mucosal surfaces
Antibodies which bind to mast cells during allergic reactions
Antibodies which can confer protection to newborn infants
Long-lived antibodies that provide long-term protection against infection
Short-lived antibodies produced during the early stages of ongoing infection
questions.explanation: Five classes of antibody are produced by activated B cells namely IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE and IgD. IgM is the first antibody produced during the early stages of ongoing infection.
questions.source_label: MRCS Part A: 550 SBAs and EMQs || 2nd Edition

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is going to work in Uganda for 6 months. As a precaution he has a Heaf (six-needle) test, and this gives a positive reaction. What is the most likely immunological significance of this result?
options: Determines exposure to Lyme disease
Determines protective antibody responses to vector-borne infections
Determines T-cell responses to the tubercle bacillus
Measures allergic responses to grass and flower pollens
No immunological significance
questions.explanation: Type IV delayed type hypersensitivity reactions come in three variants - contact, tuberculin and granulomatous all mediated by T cells. The Heaf test employs the tuberculin reaction and can be used to determine previous exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis and efficacy of vaccination.
questions.source_label: MRCS Part A: 550 SBAs and EMQs || 2nd Edition

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman, admitted for a corneal graft, will not require immunosuppressive therapy after surgery because the anterior chamber of the eye is considered to be 'immunologically privileged'. What is the most likely immunological mechanism involved?
options: Adaptive immune responses do not occur there
All immune cells are destroyed immediately upon arrival
Beneficial responses are promoted while damaging ones are suppressed
Immune cells arrive but are prevented from entering
Immune cells become functionally inactive on entering the site
questions.explanation: 'Privileged sites' were thought to be locations where immune responses did not occur. More extensive tests have revealed that these sites are not immunologically impaired but have differences in their self-regenerative capacity.
